urgency.high: Needs a human today, within hours: symptoms that could be worsening or dangerous, a child out of a critical medication within 24-48 hours, or any safety concern
urgency.medium: Should be handled within 1 business day: new but stable symptoms, a clinical question that affects care this week, results the family is worried about, a medication running out within a week
urgency.low: Routine, 2-3 business days is fine: scheduling changes, forms, records, billing, thank-you notes, general questions with no active symptoms

categories.rx_refill: Asking for a refill, renewal, or prior authorization of an existing medication
categories.medication_question: Question about dosing, side effects, stopping, or safety of a medication or vaccine
categories.new_symptom: A new illness, injury, or symptom the family wants advice about
categories.chronic_followup: An update or question about a known chronic condition (asthma, diabetes, ADHD, depression, etc.)
categories.test_results: Question about a lab, imaging, or test result, or whether a result is back
categories.scheduling: Book, move, or cancel an appointment
categories.forms_paperwork: School, sports, camp, daycare, work, or medical-clearance forms and letters
categories.referral: Status or request for a specialist referral
categories.billing_insurance: Bills, charges, coverage, or insurance questions
categories.records_request: Send or release medical or immunization records
categories.general_admin: Thank-you notes, general practice questions, confidential-care access questions, anything else

owners.nursing: RN triage pool: symptom triage, protocol refills, dosing questions, results that are back and normal, prior authorizations
owners.physician: The child's PCP: clinical decisions, abnormal results, controlled substances, mental health, anything needing medical judgment beyond a nursing protocol
owners.scheduling: Scheduling pool: booking, moving, and cancelling visits
owners.forms_desk: Referrals & forms desk: forms, letters, records release, referral status
owners.billing: Billing office: charges, statements, insurance coverage

snippets.med_list: Active medication list with doses and last-fill dates

snippets.pending_results: Ordered tests that have not resulted yet

snippets.immunizations: Immunization record and what is due

snippets.weight_dosing: Most recent weight and weight-based acetaminophen/ibuprofen dosing table
snippets.refill_protocol: Nursing refill protocol: which meds RNs may renew, controlled-substance rules, visit-required rules
snippets.referral_status: Open referrals and where each is in the process
snippets.insurance_billing: Coverage, copays, preventive-vs-sick billing rules, prior-auth process

flags.safety: The message describes a possible emergency or safety risk that needs a phone call or 911/ED advice now, not a portal reply (breathing difficulty, blue lips, head injury with vomiting or sleepiness, suicidal thoughts, anaphylaxis, seizure).
flags.multi_issue: The message contains two or more distinct requests that would normally be handled by different people or workflows (for example a refill plus a form plus a new symptom).
flags.confidential: The message involves adolescent confidential care (sexual/reproductive health, mental health, substance use) or explicitly asks that a parent not be told.
flags.frustrated: The sender expresses frustration, anger, a complaint about the practice, repeated unanswered messages, or a threat to leave.
flags.non_english: The message is written mostly in a language other than English.
flags.evisit: The family is asking for new clinical evaluation and treatment advice for a non-urgent problem that a clinician could manage through the portal without a visit (a billable e-visit).
flags.needs_reply: The sender is asking a question or requesting an action that requires a response.

Liam was seen for his asthma check on July 15, 2026, so we can renew his Flovent (fluticasone 110 mcg, 2 puffs twice a day) under our refill protocol. We're sending a 90-day supply to the CVS on Main St. Pharmacies usually have it ready within one business day, but please call ahead before Friday to be sure it's filled.

A quick reminder: take his albuterol inhaler along on the trip too, in case he needs it.

If Liam runs out before the refill is ready, or if he starts coughing, wheezing, or needs albuterol more often, please call us right away.

Safe travels!

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: I saw Ethan's lead test came back in MyChart as 6. It has a little flag next to it. Is that bad?? What are we supposed to do? We just moved into an old house.

draft.text:
Hi, thank you for reaching out — I can hear the worry, and it's a good question.

Ethan's lead level is 6 mcg/dL. The flag just means it's above the reference value of 3.5. This is not an emergency, and levels in this range usually do not cause symptoms. Most kids do well once the lead source is found and removed. His blood count (hemoglobin 11.9) was normal.

The main next steps are finding where the lead is coming from and rechecking his level. Homes built before 1978, like your 1920 rowhouse, can have lead paint or dust, especially near windows, doors, and peeling paint. Foods with iron, calcium, and vitamin C can also help.

Our nurse will contact you to set up repeat testing and share home safety and health department resources.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Sophia has had a fever up to 102.5 for 3 days now. Motrin brings it down and she's drinking OK but today she says her ear really hurts. Should we bring her in?

draft.text:
Hi, thank you for letting us know about Sophia.

A fever lasting 3 days along with new ear pain does need to be checked today. A nurse will call you within the next hour to go over her symptoms and get her into a same-day sick visit. We hold these morning appointment slots open for situations just like this one.

While you wait for our call, you can keep giving Motrin as directed on the package for her age and weight, and keep offering fluids often. It's a good sign that she is drinking well.

Please call us right away, or call 911, if Sophia has trouble breathing, becomes very hard to wake, or stops drinking.

We'll talk with you soon.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: How much children's Tylenol can I give Leo? He just turned 2 and weighs about 28 lbs. The box says to ask a doctor for under 2 so I wasn't sure.

draft.text:
Hi! Thanks for checking before giving medicine — that's a great habit.

For Leo's weight (28 lb / 12.7 kg), children's acetaminophen (Tylenol) liquid, 160 mg per 5 mL, is:

- **6 mL (190 mg) every 4 to 6 hours**
- No more than 5 doses in 24 hours

Use the syringe or cup that comes with the bottle, and double-check the bottle says 160 mg/5 mL, since strengths can differ.

If Leo is uncomfortable between doses, ibuprofen is also an option now that he's over 6 months: 6.3 mL (127 mg) of the 100 mg/5 mL liquid every 6 to 8 hours, given with food.

Please call us if his fever lasts more than 3 days, he isn't drinking, or he seems very sleepy or hard to wake.

— Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Three things: 1) Olivia needs her Focalin XR 10 refilled, she's out next week. 2) School says they need a new medication form for the nurse's office. 3) She's been getting headaches most afternoons, could that be from the medicine?

1) Refills: Focalin XR is a controlled medicine, so our nurses can't renew it. I've sent your request to Olivia's doctor to review. Her last ADHD check was June 2, and a 3-month follow-up was planned, so we may need to schedule that visit. Please let us know if you'd like help booking it.

2) School form: Her medication administration form expired, so we need a new one. I've passed this to our forms desk. You can drop off or upload the school's form, and we'll get it signed.

3) Headaches: Afternoon headaches can happen with stimulant medicines, but other things can cause them too. Please don't change her dose on your own. Let us know how often they happen, how long they last, and whether she's eating and drinking during the day. The doctor will review this with the refill, and we can set up a visit if needed.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Can I get tested for STDs without my parents finding out? Would it show up on their insurance?

draft.text:
Hi Riley,

Yes. In Pennsylvania, you can get tested and treated for STIs on your own starting at age 14. You do not need a parent's permission, and we will keep your visit and results in your confidential chart. Your parents cannot see those notes or these messages.

About insurance: if we bill your parents' plan, they may get a statement in the mail that shows a visit or lab. If you would rather avoid that, tell us when you call. We can talk about low-cost or no-cost testing options and confidential clinics in the area.

Message us back or call the office and ask for the nurse, and we will help you set up a visit. We are glad you asked.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Carter's sugars have been 280-350 all weekend even with correction doses. Ketones are small this morning. He says he feels fine. What should we do?

Because Carter's sugars have been over 300 with small ketones, we want to talk with you today. A nurse will call you within the hour. Please keep your phone nearby.

While you wait, follow the sick-day plan we went over at his last visit:
- Give extra water or sugar-free fluids to help flush the ketones.
- Give correction doses as directed by his insulin plan.
- Recheck his blood sugar and ketones every 2 to 3 hours.

Call 911 or go to the emergency room right away if Carter starts vomiting, has trouble breathing, has belly pain, or becomes very sleepy or confused.

We will follow up with you shortly.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Owen has been constipated for about 2 weeks. He only goes every 4 or 5 days and it's hard and it hurts him. We tried more water and prune juice. What else can we try?

draft.text:

Two weeks of hard, painful stools that only come every 4–5 days is something we'd like to look at. Please schedule a visit or telehealth with us in the next 1–2 days. Our scheduling team can help if you reply here or call the office.

Until then, keep up the water and prune juice. You can also offer fruits like pears, peaches, and berries, plus beans and whole grains, and let him move and play each day. A warm bath can ease the pain. Please don't start any laxative or stool softener until we talk, so we can choose the right one and dose for him.

Call us right away if Owen has belly pain that won't stop, vomiting, blood in his stool, or a fever.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Lucas fell off the monkey bars about an hour ago and hit his head. He threw up twice and now he's really sleepy. Is it OK to let him nap?
Isla's follow-up blood test was normal! Does that mean we can stop the iron drops now?

draft.text:
Hi! That's wonderful news about Isla's blood test — thank you for sticking with the iron drops.

Even when the blood count looks normal, we usually keep giving iron for another 1 to 2 months. This helps rebuild her body's iron stores so the anemia doesn't come back. So please keep giving the 15 mg iron drops once a day for now.

Isla's doctor will review her results and let you know exactly how much longer to continue and when to plan the next check. If you have not heard back in a few days, or if the drops are upsetting her stomach or causing constipation, just message us again.

Thanks for all you do to take care of her!

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Ruby has her 1 year shots next week. Is it safe for her to get the MMR when her brother is on chemo? I don't want to make him sick.

draft.text:
Hi, thank you for asking such a thoughtful question — you're looking out for both of your kids.

In general, the MMR vaccine is safe for children who live with someone getting chemotherapy. The weakened viruses in the MMR shot are not passed from the vaccinated child to other people. In fact, keeping Ruby up to date helps protect your son, because she is less likely to bring home measles, mumps, or rubella.

A few other vaccines have different rules, so we'd like to review Ruby's full 12-month vaccine list and your son's treatment plan before her visit. One of our nurses will look at her chart and follow up with you, and we can also check with your son's cancer team if that would help.

Please call us if you have questions before then.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Since starting the Symbicort Henry has been doing so much better, only needed albuterol once this month! Do we still need the follow-up in October?

draft.text:
Hi! That's wonderful news — we're so glad Henry is breathing easier and only needed his albuterol once this month.

Yes, we'd still like to keep the October 8 visit with Dr. Nguyen. That appointment was planned when we stepped up his Symbicort in July. Doing well is exactly what we hope for, and it's the reason to come in — Dr. Nguyen can check his breathing and talk about whether it's safe to lower his medicine. We don't want to change asthma treatment without a check-in first.

Please keep giving the Symbicort as prescribed until then, and keep the albuterol handy.

If Henry starts needing albuterol more often, coughing at night, or has trouble keeping up at play, message us or call sooner.

Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text: Chào bác sĩ, con tôi Bảo bị sốt 38,9 độ từ tối hôm qua và ho nhẹ. Bé vẫn ăn uống và chơi bình thường. Tôi có thể cho bé uống bao nhiêu Tylenol? Bé nặng khoảng 20 kg. Có cần đưa bé đến khám không?

draft.text:
Chào anh/chị,

Cảm ơn anh/chị đã nhắn tin. Rất mừng vì bé Bảo vẫn ăn uống và chơi bình thường — đó là dấu hiệu tốt.

Với cân nặng 20 kg, bé có thể uống Tylenol (acetaminophen) 300 mg, tức 9,4 mL loại siro 160 mg/5 mL, mỗi 4–6 giờ, tối đa 5 lần trong 24 giờ. Nếu cần, bé cũng có thể uống Ibuprofen 200 mg (10 mL loại 100 mg/5 mL) mỗi 6–8 giờ. Nhớ cho bé uống nhiều nước và nghỉ ngơi.

Hiện chưa cần đưa bé đi khám ngay. Nhưng xin gọi cho phòng khám nếu sốt kéo dài hơn 3 ngày, bé đau tai, bỏ ăn uống, hoặc trông mệt hơn nhiều. Nếu bé khó thở, môi tím tái, hoặc co giật, hãy gọi 911 ngay.

Thân mến,
Proctor Pediatrics care team
draft.text_en:
Hello,

Thank you for your message. It's good to hear that Bao is still eating and playing normally — that's a good sign.

At 20 kg, he can take Tylenol (acetaminophen) 300 mg, which is 9.4 mL of the 160 mg/5 mL liquid, every 4–6 hours, up to 5 times in 24 hours. If needed, he can also take Ibuprofen 200 mg (10 mL of the 100 mg/5 mL liquid) every 6–8 hours. Please make sure he drinks plenty of fluids and gets rest.

He does not need to be seen right away. But please call the clinic if the fever lasts more than 3 days, if he has ear pain, stops eating or drinking, or seems much more tired than usual. If he has trouble breathing, his lips turn blue, or he has a seizure, call 911 immediately.

Best regards,
Proctor Pediatrics care team

messages.text_en:
Hello Doctor,

My son Bao has had a fever of 38.9°C (102°F) since last night, along with a mild cough. He is still eating, drinking, and playing normally.

How much Tylenol can I give him? He weighs about 20 kg (about 44 lbs).

Does he need to come in to be seen?
